content: 1. It is conditionally recommended to extend tuberculosis (TB) treatment for a duration of 8 months or longer, although the certainty of evidence supporting this recommendation is very low. 2. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within two weeks of starting TB treatment, regardless of the patient’s CD4 count, for individuals living with HIV. 3. Undernutrition significantly weakens the immune system, increasing the risk of developing TB and influencing the severity and outcomes of the infection. It also raises the likelihood of drug toxicity, poor treatment adherence, relapse, and mortality, even among those undergoing treatment. 4. TB itself can lead to undernutrition, as active TB disease often causes severe weight loss due to reduced appetite, nausea, abdominal pain, nutrient losses, micronutrient deficiencies (e.g., from vomiting and diarrhea), and metabolic changes induced by the disease and its treatment (e.g., vitamin B6 deficiency from isoniazid). 5. The economic burden of TB includes direct costs (medical and non-medical expenses) and indirect costs (loss of productive time and income), which can contribute to household food insecurity. This, in turn, negatively impacts treatment adherence and outcomes. 6. Lack of adequate weight gain during TB treatment may indicate clinical severity, comorbidities, or poor treatment response, increasing the risk of death and TB relapse. Conversely, weight gain during treatment is likely a sign of positive response and may necessitate dosage adjustments for TB medications based on body weight. 7. Food and nutrition interventions, integrated into care and support services for TB patients, are cost-effective and essential for improving outcomes. Nutritional assessment should be conducted for all individuals with active TB to identify those requiring specific counseling and support. 8. Nutritional care for undernourished TB patients should be equivalent to that provided to individuals without TB but with similar nutritional status, facilitated through referrals to available nutritional services. 9. Body mass index (BMI) is the most commonly used indicator of nutritional status in adults aged 19 years and older, while BMI-for-age-and-sex Z-scores are used for individuals aged 5–18 years. For children under 5 years, weight-for-length and weight-for-height Z-scores are recommended, along with mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) measurements to identify those needing life-saving nutritional management. 10. Nutritional assessment for TB patients (and children under 5 years in their households) should occur at the start of TB treatment and be repeated regularly. This includes weight and height measurements for BMI calculation, MUAC measurements, and evaluation of recent weight loss or failure to gain weight. 11. Nutritional counseling and education should address dietary needs, meal planning, symptom management, and adherence to medications. Breastfeeding should continue for children diagnosed with TB until at least 24 months of age, alongside a diverse, age-appropriate diet. 12. Safe food preparation, storage, and hygiene practices should be emphasized, along with linkages between health clinics and community-level services, such as TB and HIV support groups. 13. Socio-economic and gender-related barriers to accessing care and adhering to treatment should be identified and addressed, including issues like unsuitable clinic hours or childcare responsibilities. 14. Nutritional support for undernourished TB patients may include ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF) combined with fortified blended foods (FBF) and facilitated access to locally available nutritious foods through cash or voucher assistance. 15. Measures to promote household food security and self-reliance should include socio-economic assessments to determine eligibility for additional support, such as in-kind or cash assistance, and community-level livelihood services like microfinance and vocational training. 16. Screening and management of comorbidities, such as diabetes mellitus, mental health disorders, and substance use disorders, should be integrated into TB care. Early diagnosis and treatment of these conditions are critical for successful TB management. 17. Smoking cessation measures should be implemented for TB patients and their close contacts, as smoking increases the risk of TB disease, relapse, and mortality by impairing local immune defenses in the airways. 18. Mental health disorders, including psychosis, depression, and anxiety, are common among TB patients and may be exacerbated by TB medications like cycloserine, isoniazid, and fluoroquinolones. Early detection and management of these conditions are essential for effective TB treatment. 19. Alcohol and substance use disorders are associated with higher risks of TB infection, disease progression, and poor treatment outcomes. Screening for these disorders should be conducted at the time of TB diagnosis, and affected individuals should receive appropriate treatment and monitoring. 20. Integrated services for TB patients who use drugs should include harm reduction measures, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of TB, and collaborative TB and HIV activities. Special efforts should be made to address stigma and ensure access to care. 21. Social protection schemes, community involvement, and the availability of clinical expertise are essential for managing TB among individuals who use drugs. Efforts should also focus on combating the cumulative stigma of TB, HIV, and drug use.
